newsitem.title: USA: US economist Kaufman sees good credit demand in 97.
newsitem.headline: US economist Kaufman sees good credit demand in 97.

text.p: A robust U.S. economy, combined with only a gradual rise of 50 to 75 basis points in short-term interest rates, suggests that demand for credit should hold steady through year end, said U.S. economist Henry Kaufman, president of Henry Kaufman and Co Inc.

"Continued strong economic growth, combined with only gradual measures by the central bank to curtail it, implies that the demand for credit should be quite good," Kaufman said, speaking before the UBS Securities Global Banking Conference here on Tuesday.
Kaufman forecast the key federal funds target rate will end 1997 about 50 to 75 basis points higher than its current level of 5.50 percent.

When asked if the Fed will tighten rates at the Federal Open Maket Committee (FOMC) meeting scheduled for May, Kaufman said the chances are even -- if the results of the April employment report on Friday showed an unemployment rate of 5.0 percent and a 250,000 increase in payrolls.
He said the Fed probably will rein in credit at the July policy meeting.
Kaufman also projected the yield on the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond should surpass 7.5 percent by year end.
"The yield curve will remain positive but will not return to the extreme positive slope that prevailed earlier in this cycle," he said.

Despite prospects for higher rates, Kaufman said both households and businesses will increase their borrowing, while banks have the liquidity and capital necessary to participate in a more active lending market.
"All this should pay off in the future growth in bank earnings, even in an environment of gradual increases in the level of U.S. interest rates," he said.
But Kaufman cautioned that recurring proposals to allow commercial ownership and control of banks would deteriorate the drive for a steady anti-inflationary monetary policy.
"If large commercial firms controlled big banks, support for a steay anti-inflationary monetary policy would wane," he said.
There is a basic difference between banking and industry, asserted Kaufman.
"Banks are the channel through which the central bank tries to achieve its objectives. By contrast, business corporations are the targets," he said.

"It is the profits that are restrained or enlarged through monetary policy. Consequently, it is in their nature to have more of an inflationary bias than independent financial institutions," he added.
